warmup.q: payments has 1,000,000 rows in 23,818 pages of 8 KB. Card 4242 has 14 payments, spread over the table. With an index on card_id, about how many pages does PostgreSQL read to fetch them?
options: About 17: a few index pages, then one table page per payment
About 1,100: the index is a twentieth of the table
All 23,818: an index helps sorting, not searching
warmup.why: The index is a tree three levels deep: one root page, one inner page and one leaf page lead to all 14 row addresses. Then each payment sits on its own table page. In the first Try it that is 3 + 14 = 17 buffers. The first option forgets the index's own pages; the third assumes the whole index is read, which only happens when the index cannot be searched.

sections.h: Without an index, finding 14 payments means reading 23,818 pages
sections.html:
The support screen looks up one card's payments: SELECT ... FROM payments WHERE card_id = 4242. On the large data set, payments has 1,000,478 rows in 23,818 pages of 8 KB, 186 MB. Card 4242 has 14 payments. Without an index, PostgreSQL has one way to find them: read every page and test every row. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) runs the query and reports what it did (trimmed, estimates removed):

 Gather (actual time=22.943..249.431 rows=14.00 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=13203 read=10615
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on payments (actual time=15.929..233.812 rows=4.67 loops=3)
         Filter: (card_id = 4242)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 333488

Each line with a name is a node, one step of the plan. The sequential scan read the table from the first page to the last. Two helper processes and the main one shared the pages (loops=3; rows=4.67 is the average per process, 14 in all), and each threw away 333,488 rows. A buffer is one 8 KB page: hit pages were already in PostgreSQL's memory, read pages came from the operating system. 23,818 pages for 14 rows: a quarter of a second here, and the cost grows with the table.

The fix you would invent: a second copy of just the card_id column, sorted, each entry holding the address of its row. The address is the row's page and its slot in the page, the ctid; card 4242's first payment lives at (339,35). In a sorted list a binary search needs 20 comparisons to find one card among a million.

Two problems remain. The copy lives in 8 KB pages too, over a thousand of them, and a binary search across pages still reads about 11 of them. Worse, a new payment's entry belongs somewhere in the middle, and keeping the list sorted would mean shifting every entry after it.

So leave free space in each page, so that a new entry usually fits where it belongs, and put a small directory on top: one entry per page, saying where its keys start. The directory needs pages too, so it gets a directory of its own, until a single page, the root, covers everything. When a page fills up, it splits in two and its parent gets one more entry. Every lookup walks from the root down to one leaf. That is a B-tree, PostgreSQL's default index, more exactly a B+tree; the database internals track builds one in "B+trees".

CREATE INDEX payments_card_idx ON payments (card_id) builds one in about two seconds: a root page with 4 entries, 4 inner pages and 1,130 leaf pages. Card 4242 now costs 3 index pages plus the 14 table pages its rows are on, 17 buffers and a quarter of a millisecond. In Kotlin terms:

val byCard = TreeMap<Long, MutableList<RowAddress>>()   // the index: sorted keys, row addresses
byCard[4242L]                                            // a seek: 3 pages, then 14 addresses
payments.filter { it.cardId == 4242L }                   // no index: test all 1,000,478 rows

That is the picture for this lesson: an index is a sorted copy of a few columns, each entry pointing to its row, and a query is fast when it can find one short run of entries in that copy.

try.title: A seek instead of a scan
steps: This Try it uses the large data set. If an earlier lesson did not load it, load it now from the labs folder (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course -f /seed/load-big.sql, about a minute), then open psql: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the block. Read the first plan: how many rows did the scan remove, and how many buffers did it touch?
The CREATE INDEX takes a few seconds. Compare the second plan's buffers with the first's, then check the number of levels and the sizes.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SET search_path = big, public; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments WHERE card_id = 4242; CREATE INDEX payments_card_idx ON payments (card_id); EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments WHERE card_id = 4242; SELECT level + 1 AS levels FROM bt_metap('payments_card_idx'); SELECT relname, relpages, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size FROM pg_class WHERE relname IN ('payments', 'payments_card_idx') AND relnamespace = 'big'::regnamespace;

sections.h: Read EXPLAIN from the innermost node out
sections.html:
A plan is a tree. Each node produces rows and hands them to the node above it, and the top node hands them to you. So read a plan from the most indented node upward, in the direction the rows flow. The stepper walks through the plan for card 4242's payments joined to their merchants, newest first. Four kinds of numbers tell you nearly everything:

  • rows is what the node produced per loop, and loops is how many times it ran. Multiply them: the merchants Index Scan ran 14 times and found one row each time.
  • Buffers counts pages for the node and everything under it. The Nested Loop's 59 is the payments side's 17 plus the merchants side's 42. The top node's buffers are the query's total.
  • cost=4.51..47.94 rows=11 is the planner's estimate, made before the query ran, in arbitrary units. Compare its rows with the actual rows. A miss by ten times or more means the plan was chosen from wrong numbers.
  • Index Cond is a condition used to search the index. Filter is checked row by row after the rows were read, and Rows Removed by Filter counts the wasted work.

Three scan nodes come up all the time. An Index Scan follows each index entry to its row at once, in index order, which is how it can return rows already sorted. A Bitmap Index Scan first collects all the matching row addresses; the Bitmap Heap Scan above it sorts them by page and reads each table page once. PostgreSQL picks the bitmap when it expects more than a few rows, or rows spread over many pages: here, 14 rows on 14 different pages. An Index Only Scan answers from the index without touching the table; the next section builds one.

PostgreSQL 18 changed EXPLAIN in small ways you will see everywhere: EXPLAIN ANALYZE includes buffer counts without being asked, rows have two decimals because they are averages over loops, and each index scan reports Index Searches, the number of times it descended the tree.

Plain EXPLAIN prints the estimates without running anything, so it is safe on any statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs it: on an UPDATE it updates the rows, so wrap it in BEGIN and ROLLBACK.

sections.h: Column order decides which queries a multicolumn index serves
sections.html:
The merchant dashboard shows one merchant's newest payments in a month:

SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments
WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Without an index, PostgreSQL reads all 23,818 pages and sorts merchant 1000's 22 September payments: about 0.7 seconds. An index on both columns fixes it, but the order of the columns matters. A multicolumn index sorts by its first column, and by the second only among entries with the same first column, like a phone book sorted by surname and then by first name.

With (created_at, merchant_id), September is one long run of about 100,000 entries from every merchant, sorted by time. Merchant 1000's entries are scattered through it. PostgreSQL walks the run backward from 1 October and checks each entry's merchant until it has 20: 397 pages, 11 ms.

With (merchant_id, created_at), all of merchant 1000's entries sit together, already in time order, and its September is one short stretch. PostgreSQL descends to the last of them and reads 20 entries backward: 23 pages, a tenth of a millisecond. Both plans list both columns under Index Cond, so judge them by their buffers. The rule: equality columns first, then the column you range over or sort by. In Kotlin terms it is a TreeMap keyed by compareBy({ it.merchantId }, { it.createdAt }), where the range from (1000, 1 September) to (1000, 1 October) is one contiguous subMap. Swap the key's parts and no contiguous slice holds just merchant 1000.

PostgreSQL 18 softens the rule with skip scan. An index on (status, created_at) used to be useless for a query on created_at alone, because created_at is sorted only inside each status. Now PostgreSQL jumps into each status's part of the index and searches created_at there. For five minutes of payments it reported Index Searches: 7 and read 27 pages, where a sequential scan reads 23,818. It pays off only when the leading column has few distinct values: through (merchant_id, created_at) the same query took 1,616 searches and 5,243 pages.

An index can also carry columns it does not sort by. INCLUDE (status, amount_minor) stores them in the leaf entries, so a query that needs nothing else, such as merchant 1000's September gross, runs as an Index Only Scan and never reads the table: 4 pages. PostgreSQL may skip the table only for pages its visibility map marks as all-visible, and VACUUM keeps that map up to date. Heap Fetches counts the rows it still had to check in the table.

sections.h: PostgreSQL cannot search an index for a value it has to compute
sections.html:
An index on created_at is sorted by created_at. It is not sorted by created_at::date, or lower(email), or anything else computed from the column, so PostgreSQL cannot search it for those values. Queries that look harmless hit this all the time.

WHERE created_at::date = '2026-09-01' read the whole index on created_at, 2,739 pages, casting each value and filtering: the plan says Filter, not Index Cond. The same day as a range on the bare column, created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02', read 13 pages. A condition that can search an index is called sargable, from "search argument". Keep the column alone on one side and put the computation on the constants.

The cast can come from your own code. PostgreSQL compares a bigint with a numeric by converting the bigint, so WHERE payment_id = $1 with a numeric parameter, which is what JDBC's setBigDecimal sends, runs as (payment_id)::numeric = $1. The primary key goes unused and one lookup by id reads all 23,818 pages. Bind ids with setLong. Oracle has the same trap when a VARCHAR2 column meets an NVARCHAR bind.

When you cannot change the query, index the expression. CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email)) turns the case-insensitive login lookup from 532 pages into 4. The expression must be immutable, always the same result for the same input. created_at::date is not, since its result depends on the session's TimeZone, so PostgreSQL refuses to index it.

Sometimes the planner skips an index on purpose. 93% of payments are succeeded, so WHERE status = 'succeeded' needs almost every table page anyway. Reading the table straight through beats jumping between index and table 930,000 times, and the plan is a sequential scan even with an index on status. The same index is used for status = 'pending', 1% of rows. If only the rare value is ever queried, a partial index stores only those rows: CREATE INDEX ON payments (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending' is 232 kB, against 21 MB for an index on created_at over every payment.

sections.h: Every index costs something on every write
sections.html:
An index is a second copy, so every write pays for it. An INSERT adds an entry to every index. An UPDATE adds entries too, unless it changes no indexed column and the new row version fits on the same page. Dead entries stay until VACUUM removes them. Copying 200,000 payments into a table with no index wrote 42 MB of write-ahead log; into the same table with a primary key and three more indexes it wrote 99 MB, and the indexes took 22 MB next to the 37 MB table. On a quiet run the copy took about 3 seconds bare and 8 with the four indexes, and 13 once a GIN index on metadata (lesson 10) was added.

So index what the queries need, and find out what they need with pg_stat_statements, which the course's Compose service preloads. It records each statement with its constants replaced by $1, how often it ran, its total and mean time, and the pages it touched. Twenty card lookups become one line with calls = 20 and 23,818 pages per call. Sort the view by total_exec_time: a query that takes 2 ms but runs a million times a day costs more than a slow nightly report. Take the top one, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) it, find the sequential scan or the Filter that removes most rows, and build the index whose leading columns are its equality conditions.

Check the other direction too. pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan counts how often each index has been used; one still at 0 after a month of production traffic only costs writes. Foreign keys deserve a look of their own: PostgreSQL never indexes the referencing column for you, and the course schema deliberately left those indexes for this lesson. Without an index on payments.merchant_id, deleting a merchant makes PostgreSQL scan payments for rows that still point to it.

try.title: What an index costs, and which query needs one
steps: This uses the large data set.
Run the block. It copies 200,000 payments twice, once into a bare table and once into the same table with four indexes, and prints how much write-ahead log each copy wrote.
Then it resets pg_stat_statements, runs 20 card lookups with \gexec (one line of output each), and asks which query cost the most.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SET search_path = big, public; CREATE TABLE pay_copy (LIKE payments); SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE payment_id <= 200000; -- warm the source pages \timing on SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset INSERT INTO pay_copy SELECT * FROM payments WHERE payment_id <= 200000; SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), :'before')) AS wal_written; TRUNCATE pay_copy; ALTER TABLE pay_copy ADD PRIMARY KEY (payment_id); CREATE INDEX ON pay_copy (card_id); CREATE INDEX ON pay_copy (merchant_id, created_at); CREATE INDEX ON pay_copy (created_at); SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset INSERT INTO pay_copy SELECT * FROM payments WHERE payment_id <= 200000; SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), :'before')) AS wal_written; \timing off SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('pay_copy')) AS table_size, pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('pay_copy')) AS four_indexes; DROP TABLE pay_copy; SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset() IS NOT NULL AS reset; SELECT format('SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE card_id = %s', 4000 + g) FROM generate_series(1, 20) AS g \gexec SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time) AS mean_ms, (shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read) / calls AS pages_per_call, query FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE query LIKE '%card_id%' ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 3;

try.expect:
wal_written is about 42 MB for the copy without indexes and 99 MB with four, and the four indexes take 22 MB next to the 37 MB table. The two insert times are less steady: on a busy Docker VM they swing by seconds from run to run, so trust the WAL and the sizes. The \gexec line runs 20 card lookups (20 one-row results, trimmed here), and pg_stat_statements folds them into one line:

 calls | mean_ms | pages_per_call |                      query
-------+---------+----------------+--------------------------------------------------
    20 |     240 |          23818 | SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE card_id = $1
(1 row)

mean_ms varies with the machine. pages_per_call is the whole table, every time: this query wants the index from the first Try it.

analogy: An index is the index at the back of a book. To find every page that mentions "chargeback" you do not read the book; you look the word up in the alphabetical list, which sends you to pages 12, 87 and 340. A multicolumn index is a list sorted by chapter and then by word: it finds "chargeback in chapter 4" at once, but not "chargeback in any chapter", because that word is scattered through every chapter's section. A partial index covers only the words of one chapter, an index on an expression lists the words in lower case, and a covering index also prints the sentence next to each entry so you never open the page. The analogy breaks on cost: a printed index is written once, while a database index is rewritten on every INSERT and every UPDATE of its columns, and PostgreSQL decides for itself, by estimates, whether looking something up is cheaper than reading straight through.
world: Most slow endpoints in a payments service are one missing or misordered index away from fast: the merchant dashboard (merchant_id, created_at), the card history (card_id, created_at), the idempotency lookup on payment_uid, the outbox poller on (status, created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'. pg_stat_statements is the place to start, and on Oracle the same question is answered by AWR's SQL ordered by elapsed time. Watch the JVM side for the hidden cast: a Kotlin BigDecimal id bound with setBigDecimal, or a Hibernate mapping of a NUMBER column to BigDecimal, makes PostgreSQL convert the column and skip the primary key. Every index also slows the Kafka consumer that inserts payments at 5,000 a second and grows the WAL that your replicas must replay and your CDC pipeline (Debezium) must read through, so drop indexes that pg_stat_user_indexes says nobody uses. In production, build them with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which does not block writes, in a Flyway migration that does not run inside a transaction.
mistake: Adding an index and assuming the query uses it, without reading the plan. People do it because the index exists, the column is in the WHERE clause, and the query got faster in development on a few hundred rows, where every plan is fast. In production the condition casts the column (created_at::date, a numeric bind on a bigint key), the columns are in the wrong order for the equality and range conditions, or the value matches most of the table, and the plan is still a sequential scan or a full index scan behind a Filter. The fix is to read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on production-sized data: the condition should appear as an Index Cond, the buffers should be in the tens rather than the thousands, and rows removed by filter should be near zero.

compare.title: Actual rows and buffers for one query: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle: run with statistics, then DISPLAY_CURSOR
a.html: -- run the query once, collecting row-source statistics SELECT /*+ gather_plan_statistics */ payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 00:00:00 +00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-10-01 00:00:00 +00:00' ORDER BY created_at DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY; -- the plan of this session's last statement, with -- E-Rows (estimated), A-Rows (actual) and Buffers SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
b.html: -- runs the query and prints the plan with estimated -- and actual rows, loops and buffers on every node -- (BUFFERS is included by default since PostgreSQL 18) EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; -- plain EXPLAIN: estimates only, nothing runs

compare.note: Both databases separate the estimate from the measurement. Oracle's EXPLAIN PLAN, like PostgreSQL's plain EXPLAIN, shows only what the optimizer expects; the actual rows and buffers come from running the statement with statistics collection on and reading the cursor's plan with DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR, where E-Rows against A-Rows plays the role of PostgreSQL's rows=11 against actual rows=14.00. Both print a tree as indented operations, read from the innermost outward. The index rules carry over: Oracle B-tree indexes follow the same column-order rule, Oracle has had an INDEX SKIP SCAN for many releases, its function-based indexes are PostgreSQL's expression indexes, and since Oracle has no INCLUDE clause, a covering index there simply adds the extra columns to the key.

worked.title: An index for the account statement, from a slow query to an Index Only Scan

steps.say: The statement page lists one account's ledger entries for a month, oldest first. pg_stat_statements puts it near the top by total time. On the large data set the ledger has 3,398,299 rows in 33,630 pages, and the plan reads all of them to return 4:
steps.code: -- 1. the query and its plan (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF), trimmed) SELECT created_at, entry_type, amount_minor FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = 4242 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01' ORDER BY created_at; -- Sort (actual time=224.879..229.448 rows=4.00 loops=1) -- Buffers: shared hit=285 read=33348 -- -> Gather -- -> Parallel Seq Scan on ledger_entries (... rows=1.33 loops=3) -- Filter: ((created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...) AND (account_id = 4242)) -- Rows Removed by Filter: 1132826

steps.say: Choose the key from the conditions. account_id is an equality, so it goes first. created_at is both the range and the sort order, so it goes second: then the month is one contiguous run, already in the order the page wants, and the Sort disappears.
steps.code: -- 2. equality column first, then the range and sort column CREATE INDEX ledger_account_created_idx ON ledger_entries (account_id, created_at);

steps.say: The query also returns entry_type and amount_minor. Each one found through the index would still cost a visit to a table page. Carry them in the leaf entries with INCLUDE, so the index alone answers the query.
steps.code: -- 3. the same key, plus the returned columns in the leaves CREATE INDEX ledger_account_created_idx ON ledger_entries (account_id, created_at) INCLUDE (entry_type, amount_minor);

steps.say: Check the plan, not the clock: an Index Only Scan with both conditions in Index Cond, no Sort, no Filter, Heap Fetches: 0 and 7 buffers instead of 33,633. The bill comes with it: on the large data set the index is 161 MB next to a 263 MB table, written on every ledger insert. For a page every customer opens, that is a fair price. For a report run once a month, it is not.
steps.code: -- 4. the new plan (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF), trimmed) -- Index Only Scan using ledger_account_created_idx on ledger_entries (actual time=7.463..7.468 rows=4.00 loops=1) -- Index Cond: ((account_id = 4242) AND (created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...)) -- Heap Fetches: 0 -- Index Searches: 1 -- Buffers: shared hit=4 read=3 SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ledger_account_created_idx')) AS idx, -- 161 MB pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ledger_entries')) AS tbl; -- 263 MB

lab.title: Three indexes and one rewrite, checked against the plan
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. Five of the seven fail. The two that check the rows of payments_on_day already pass: its placeholder returns the right rows, the slow way.

The tests build a 200,000-row copy of payments once (schema lab11, vacuumed), run your statement on it inside a transaction that is rolled back, and read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). A failure prints the whole plan.
merchant_month_index.sql builds an index with the right columns in the wrong order. Fix the order so the dashboard query reads at most 40 buffers, with no Sort.
payments_on_day.sql casts created_at to a date. Rewrite the condition so an index on created_at can search it, keeping both edges of the day right.
merchant_gross_index.sql builds an index that finds the rows but cannot answer the query alone. Make the monthly statement an Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0. Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Equality first: CREATE INDEX payments_merchant_month_idx ON payments (merchant_id, created_at);. Read the failing plan's buffers before and after.
WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2026-03-12 00:00+00' AND created_at < timestamptz '2026-03-13 00:00+00': half-open, so midnight is in, 23:59:59.5 is in, and the 13th is out.

The query reads merchant_id, created_at, status and amount_minor. Keep the first two as the key and add INCLUDE (status, amount_minor). The second test adds five rows on a page VACUUM has not seen, so a few heap fetches are expected there.

drill.title: Pick the index, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the index for each query and say which plan node you expect. (1) WHERE card_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10. (2) WHERE lower(email) = lower(?) on customers. (3) WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '15 minutes', where 1% of payments are pending. (4) SELECT sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = ? AND created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?. Then rewrite WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-03-12' so an index on created_at can serve it.

answer.html: -- (1) equality, then the sort column: Index Scan Backward, no Sort, stops after 10 CREATE INDEX ON payments (card_id, created_at); -- (2) index the expression the query uses: Index Scan (or Bitmap) with Index Cond on lower(email) CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email)); -- (3) a partial index holds only the 1% that is ever queried: small, and an Index Scan CREATE INDEX ON payments (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; -- (4) key for the search, INCLUDE for the sum: Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches near 0 after VACUUM CREATE INDEX ON payments (merchant_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount_minor); -- the rewrite: the bare column, a half-open range WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2026-03-12 00:00+00' AND created_at < timestamptz '2026-03-13 00:00+00'

recap: An index is a sorted copy of some columns with each row's address. A B-tree of three levels finds a key in 3 page reads, then one table page per row; without it, PostgreSQL reads the whole table.
Read EXPLAIN from the most indented node up. rows is per loop, so multiply by loops; Buffers include the children; compare estimated rows with actual rows; Index Cond searches, Filter only discards.

In a multicolumn index, equality columns come first, then the range or sort column. PostgreSQL 18's skip scan helps when the leading column has few values. INCLUDE columns make an Index Only Scan possible.

A function or cast on the column (created_at::date, a numeric bind on a bigint) stops the index search: keep the bare column on one side, or index the expression. Low-selectivity conditions are rightly scanned; partial indexes cover the rare values.
Every index is written on every insert and most updates: more WAL, more space. Choose indexes from pg_stat_statements and drop the ones pg_stat_user_indexes says are unused.

explain.prompt: A teammate added an index on payments(created_at) for the daily settlement report, which filters with WHERE created_at::date = :day, and the report is as slow as before. Explain what is happening and what you would change, and how you would prove the fix with EXPLAIN.
explain.answer: The index is a sorted copy of created_at values. The report compares created_at::date, a value computed from each row, and the index is not sorted by that, so PostgreSQL cannot seek to the day's first entry. It either scans the table or reads the entire index and casts every value, and the plan shows the condition as a Filter with hundreds of thousands of rows removed: on the course's large data set that was 2,739 pages for one day. An index on the expression would fix the search, but created_at::date depends on the session time zone, so PostgreSQL refuses to index it. The clean fix is to rewrite the condition as a half-open range on the bare column: created_at >= :day and created_at < :day + 1, with the boundaries computed in UTC or the business time zone in the application. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) then shows an Index Scan or Index Only Scan with both bounds under Index Cond, no Filter on created_at, and buffers in the tens: 13 pages in the course's run. I would check it on production-sized data, because on a small table every plan looks fast.

deeper.html:
BRIN is a different kind of index for tables whose physical order follows a column. It stores only the minimum and maximum of each range of pages, 128 pages by default, so a BRIN index on payments(created_at), whose rows were inserted in time order, is 24 kB instead of 21 MB, and a time-range query skips every page range that cannot match. It is useless when the order is mixed, as it is for ledger_entries.created_at in the large data set, which was loaded by entry type. pg_stats.correlation tells you which case you are in: 0.999 for payments.created_at, 0.314 for the ledger's. Near 1 or -1 suits BRIN.

GIN, from lesson 10, is an inverted index: one entry per key or value found inside a document or array, each with the list of rows that contain it. It answers @> and friends, and it pays for that on writes; its fastupdate buffer of pending entries hides part of the cost until VACUUM or a full buffer merges them.

The planner's estimates come from statistics that ANALYZE (and autovacuum) collect: a sample of each column's values, its most common values, a histogram, the number of distinct values. When two columns are correlated, say merchant_id and country, the planner multiplies their selectivities as if they were independent and underestimates. CREATE STATISTICS on the pair fixes that. The database internals track's "Query optimization and cardinality estimates" builds the estimator itself.

In production, CREATE INDEX blocks writes to the table for as long as it runs. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not, at the price of two passes over the table and the rule that it cannot run inside a transaction block, so a Flyway migration that uses it must be marked non-transactional. If it fails halfway, it leaves an INVALID index behind that you must drop.

auto_explain logs the plan of every statement slower than a threshold, with auto_explain.log_analyze for actual rows. It is the way to catch the plan of a query that is only slow in production, at 3 a.m., with that day's data.
